strengths: Immediate removal of a registered bike from the available list, and protection against two bikers registering the same bike, both through one local transaction (alternative_evaluation.json A1/S7 satisfied).
Rentals, expiry jobs and Payments work in one process, so no distributed coordination is needed whichever payment timing is decided (A1 driver 'Rental lifecycle and time-based charging' satisfied).
Smallest runtime and operational footprint of the three; the only alternative rated satisfied on 'Low carbon footprint' (qualitative).
Simplest privacy posture: personal and usage data live in one store without replicated read models (QA Privacy positive).
Payment and SMS/email providers are isolated behind adapters with circuit breakers (Interoperability and Modifiability positive).
weaknesses: S6 is only partially satisfied: no element is identified for navigation to the selected bike.
S1 is only partially satisfied: TLS terminates at the gateway, and encryption from there to the database is not described.
No architectural support for 'Ease of use for all riders' (unclear), and no client-specific shaping for web versus mobile (Portability neutral).
Reporting and history queries run against the transactional database, relying on assumption S2-G5.
qa_tensions: Performance versus Sustainability: one shared database keeps the footprint low and availability immediate, but bulk location updates and reporting queries compete for it (qualitative; no load data).
Availability versus Sustainability and simplicity: one deployable unit minimises components but means all capabilities fail and redeploy together.
Modifiability now versus later: in-process scheduling is simple today, but adding asynchronous behaviour later needs refactoring.
arch_tradeoff: Trades fault isolation and independent scaling for strong consistency and minimal infrastructure.
Trades client-tailored APIs (no BFF) for a single, thin security boundary.
risks: If fleet size or the rate of location updates is larger than expected, the shared database may become a bottleneck (unmeasured; depends on S2-G1, S1-G49).
Overload or a defect in Reporting can degrade bike search and rental (A1 limitation).
Whole-unit redeploys may conflict with an availability target that has not been stated (S2-G2, S1-G50).

strengths: Strongest fault isolation: a payment-provider or service outage need not stop bike search (QA Availability positive; driver 'Service availability to riders' satisfied).
The Fleet & Availability service scales independently with location traffic.
CQRS read models keep history and hourly/daily aggregates off the transactional path (S11, S13 satisfied).
Matches the infrastructure the project description lists as available (container orchestration, registry, broker, tracing; S1-G53 marks this as permissive, not mandatory).
weaknesses: S7 is unclear: removal from the available list is eventually consistent, which relies on assumption S2-G7 because 'as soon as' is not quantified.
Driver 'Timely bike availability and location tracking' (high priority) is only partially satisfied, the worst result on that driver among the three alternatives.
Driver 'Rental lifecycle and time-based charging' is partially satisfied: saga compensations cannot be defined until payment timing is decided (S2-G15).
Driver 'Low carbon footprint' is not satisfied (stated by A2 itself); QA Sustainability is negative.
S1 and S6 are only partially satisfied (no device-to-database encryption described; no navigation element).
qa_tensions: Availability and scalability versus Sustainability: fault isolation comes with the highest infrastructure footprint.
Availability versus Performance (timeliness) and Usability: asynchronous events isolate services but make availability eventually consistent, so riders may briefly see bikes that are already taken.
Security and Privacy scoping versus attack surface: data is confined per service, but more channels and replicated read models widen what must be protected and erased.
arch_tradeoff: Trades consistency and simplicity for independent deployability, scaling and fault isolation.
Requires Saga, Service Registry and CQRS as consequences of distribution, adding design work that depends on unresolved requirements (payment timing).
risks: The organisation may not be able to operate orchestration, broker, registry and tracing (S2-G6).
The higher footprint may not be justified by actual scale or availability needs, which are unknown (S2-G9).
Saga design may need rework once the timing of payment relative to unlock is decided (S2-G15).
GDPR erasure must be propagated across services and read models (S2-G17).

strengths: Best coverage of the requirements: 12 of 13 satisfied. S6 is satisfied because the mobile BFF explicitly covers code scanning and navigation; S1 is partial, as in all alternatives (alternative_evaluation.json A3).
Keeps A1's transactional guarantee for S6/S7 (immediate removal from availability, protection against concurrent registration) while moving notifications and reporting to events.

Reporting uses CQRS read models, removing A1's dependency on assumption S2-G5 and its contention between reporting and rider flows; aggregated read models also allow minimised administrator data (S1-G35).
The only alternative with an architectural element for 'Ease of use for all riders' (partially satisfied) and positive Portability, through client-specific BFFs.
The transactional outbox makes delivery of verification and expiry notifications reliable after the core transaction commits.
weaknesses: S1 is only partially satisfied: the BFFs are the security boundary, and encryption from them to the database is not described.
Edge security must be implemented consistently in two BFFs (QA Security mixed).
Read models replicate usage data, so retention and erasure rules must also cover them (QA Privacy mixed; S2-G17).
More components than A1 (two BFFs plus a broker): 'Low carbon footprint' is only partially satisfied, and QA Sustainability is mixed.
The core still scales and fails as one unit ('Service availability to riders' partially satisfied).
Mobile access to history downloads is not described; the web BFF holds them (A3/S11 rationale).
qa_tensions: Portability and Usability versus Security: tailoring each client means two edge boundaries to secure and keep consistent.
Performance (decoupled reporting) versus Privacy: read models remove load from the transactional store but replicate usage data.
Reliability of side effects versus Sustainability and simplicity: the broker and outbox add components and implementation complexity (idempotent consumers).

Timeliness of side effects: verification and expiry notifications and the administrator status refresh lag by the event propagation delay. This matters for the verification code only under the 30-second reading of S2 (S1-G4); qualitative, unmeasured.
arch_tradeoff: Trades A1's minimal footprint for client-specific APIs and asynchronous side effects, while keeping the critical rental transaction local.
Trades A2's fault isolation and independent scaling of the core for strong consistency and a single deployable core.
risks: Two BFFs may not be justified if web and mobile flows turn out not to differ much (S2-G10).
Running a message broker may not be acceptable for the deployment (S2-G11).
Outbox and consumer implementation errors could cause notifications or usage records to be duplicated or missing (implementation complexity noted by A3; no measured evidence).
Location updates still go to the single core database; the scale is unknown (S2-G1, S1-G49).
